a: a pattern of repentance
p: The Greek calls Enoch an example of repentance; manuscript B calls him a sign of knowledge; the Masada scroll has no text of the verse.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (300s AD), as printed by Swete; Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus agree (Swete's notes give no difference)
readings.en: an example of repentance to the generations
readings.plain: a pattern of repentance

readings.w: Cairo Genizah manuscript B (medieval), folio XIII verso, line 18
readings.en: a sign of knowledge for generation after generation
readings.plain: a sign of knowledge

readings.w: Latin Vulgate (Old Latin): 'translatus est in paradisum, ut det gentibus poenitentiam'
readings.orig: translatus est in paradisum, ut det gentibus poenitentiam
readings.en: was carried off into paradise, to give repentance to the nations
readings.plain: a pattern of repentance, carried off into paradise to bring the nations to repentance

why: The Plain follows the Greek, the base text of this site's Sirach. The Hebrew 'sign of knowledge' fits the Enoch traditions of 1 Enoch, where Enoch is the scribe who learns heaven's secrets; the Greek 'repentance' may reflect a reading of Enoch's walking with God as a turning to God.
b: The Masada scroll, column VII, goes from 44:15 (line 22) to 44:17 (line 24) in Eric Reymond's transcription, and line 23 is empty. Whether the empty line is a space left on purpose or not, Masada has no text of 44:16. Rendsburg and Binstein date the Qumran and Masada copies between about 50 BC and AD 70. 49:14 has a second Enoch verse. The Latin adds 'into paradise'.

a: and so the flood came
t: Why or when the flood came
p: Vaticanus says 'because of this the flood came'; Alexandrinus 'when the flood came'; manuscript B 'by his covenant the flood ended'.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.en: because of this there came a flood
readings.plain: and so the flood came

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus and a corrector of Sinaiticus (Swete's notes: ὅτε for the second διὰ τοῦτο); KJV
readings.en: when the flood came
readings.plain: when the flood came

readings.w: Cairo Genizah manuscript B, folio XIV recto, line 2
readings.en: and by his covenant the flood ceased
readings.plain: and by the covenant with him the flood came to an end

why: The Plain keeps Vaticanus, the base text, though its sense is awkward ('so', that is, this is how the flood came to leave a remnant). The Alexandrinus reading is smoother and the KJV follows it. The Hebrew says something different: the flood stopped because of God's covenant with Noah.

a: In his commandments he gave him
t: Gave him, or gave to him?
p: Vaticanus has 'he gave him' (accusative); Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus and manuscript B have 'he gave to him'.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (Swete's notes: αυτω ℵA, and εν ταις εντ. A); manuscript B, folio XV recto, line 7, 'and he gave him all his commandments' (ויתן לו כל מצותיו)
readings.orig: ἔδωκεν αὐτῷ ἐν ταῖς ἐντολαῖς αὐτοῦ
readings.en: he gave to him in his commandments
readings.plain: In his commandments he gave him

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.en: he gave him (over) in his commandments
readings.plain: He gave him over to his commandments

why: The Plain departs from Vaticanus. Its accusative 'him' gives no clear sense with 'authority' that follows; the dative of Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus, 'gave to him', matches manuscript B's 'gave him'.
b: Sinaiticus has the dative too, but 'his commandments' without 'in' (εντολας).

a: His Lord loved Samuel,
p: Vaticanus does not name Samuel here; Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Ephraemi and manuscript B do. Goes with the next entry.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus and Ephraemi (Swete's notes: + Σαμουηλ); manuscript B, folio XVI recto, line 12 (שמואל)
readings.en: loved by his Lord, Samuel
readings.plain: His Lord loved Samuel,

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.en: loved by his Lord
readings.plain: His Lord loved him,

why: The Plain departs from Vaticanus here. Three of the four great Greek codices and the Hebrew name Samuel, and without the name the reader cannot tell who is meant; Vaticanus omits it.

a: who set up the kingdom
p: Vaticanus has 'set up a king'; the other codices and manuscript B 'the kingdom'. Goes with the entry before.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus and Ephraemi (Swete's notes: βασιλειαν); manuscript B 'established a kingdom' (הכין ממלכת)
readings.en: established a kingdom
readings.plain: who set up the kingdom

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.en: established a king
readings.plain: who set up a king

why: The Plain follows the codices that agree with the Hebrew, as in the line before. The meaning is close: Samuel anointed Saul (1 Samuel 10:1) and so founded the monarchy.

a: his faithfulness made him known
t: By his faithfulness or by his words?
p: Vaticanus repeats 'faithfulness'; the other codices and manuscript B have 'by his words'.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.en: he was known by his faithfulness
readings.plain: his faithfulness made him known

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus and Ephraemi (Swete's notes: ῥήμασιν); manuscript B 'by his word' (בדברו)
readings.en: he was known by his words
readings.plain: his words made him known

why: The Plain keeps Vaticanus, since both readings make sense. The second reading has strong support and may well be original; the repeated word in Vaticanus could be a copyist's echo of the line before.

a: the leaders of the people of Tyre
p: The Greek has Tyrians; manuscript B has 'the governors of the enemy'. The Hebrew word for 'enemy' and 'Tyre' looks the same.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.en: leaders of the Tyrians
readings.plain: the leaders of the people of Tyre

readings.w: Cairo Genizah manuscript B, folio XVI recto, line 18
readings.en: the governors of the enemy
readings.plain: the commanders of the enemy

why: The Plain follows the Greek. In unpointed Hebrew צר can be read tsar, 'enemy', or Tsor, 'Tyre'. 1 Samuel 7 says nothing of Tyre, so the Hebrew 'enemy' is probably what Ben Sira meant and the Greek translator misread it.

a: and lift up the horn of his people
t: To lift up, or he will lift up?
p: Vaticanus has a future, 'he will lift up'; the other Greek codices, the Latin and manuscript B have 'to lift up'.

readings.w: Codices Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus and Ephraemi (Swete's notes: ανυψωσαι ℵAC); Latin 'et exaltare cornu gentis suae' (47:6 in its numbering); manuscript B, folio XVI verso, line 10, 'and to raise the horn of his people' (ולהרים את קרן עמו)
readings.en: to lift up the horn of his people
readings.plain: and lift up the horn of his people

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.en: he will lift up the horn of his people
readings.plain: He will lift up the horn of his people.

why: The Plain follows the infinitive, which carries on from 'to bring down a man of war'. The difference in sense is small.
b: In the same verse Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Ephraemi and a corrector of Vaticanus add δυνατόν, 'a mighty man of war'; the Plain keeps Vaticanus there.

a: and those made beautiful by love
t: Adorned by love, or by your love?
p: A corrector of Sinaiticus and the Latin read 'by your love'; the KJV, from a different text, 'slept in love'.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.en: those adorned with love
readings.plain: and those made beautiful by love

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus as corrected (Swete's notes: αγαπησι σου); Latin Vulgate 'in amicitia tua decorati sunt'
readings.en: those adorned with your love
readings.plain: and those made beautiful by your love

readings.w: KJV 'and slept in love'
readings.orig: (not in Swete's Greek; the KJV followed a different text)
readings.en: and slept in love
readings.plain: and those who fell asleep in love

why: The Plain keeps Vaticanus. Manuscript B is too damaged here to help (see the note on this verse).

a: For we too will indeed live.
p: The Greek hopes 'we too will live'; the Latin adds a line that denies it: after death our name will not be the same.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (300s AD), as printed by Swete; Alexandrinus has ζωῆς
readings.en: for we too shall live with life (that is, we shall indeed live)
readings.plain: For we too will indeed live.

readings.w: Latin Vulgate (48:12 in its numbering)
readings.orig: Nam nos vita vivimus tantum: post mortem autem non erit tale nomen nostrum
readings.en: For we live only in life; but after death our name will not be such
readings.plain: For we live only this life, and after death our name will not be the same.

why: The Plain follows the Greek. The Latin line is not in the Greek or, as far as it survives, in manuscript B, whose end of the line Abegg and Parker restore as 'we shall live'.

a: led water inside it
p: Vaticanus reads 'brought Gog into their midst', a slip; Alexandrinus and manuscript B have water.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (Swete's notes: υδωρ; αυτης); manuscript B 'bringing water into its midst', folio XVIII recto, line 8
readings.en: brought water into its midst
readings.plain: led water inside it

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.orig: εἰσήγαγεν εἰς μέσον αὐτῶν τὸν Γώγ
readings.en: brought Gog into their midst
readings.plain: led Gog in among them

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus as corrected (Swete's notes: τ. αγωγον)
readings.en: the conduit
readings.plain: led the conduit inside it

why: The Plain departs from Vaticanus. 'Gog', the enemy of Ezekiel 38–39, makes no sense here; Alexandrinus and the Hebrew (בהטות אל תוכה מים) have water, which fits Hezekiah's tunnel (2 Kings 20:20). Sinaiticus's first hand had another garbled word, τὸν Ηωγ.

a: he remembered the enemies with a downpour
p: Manuscript B names Job here; the Greek has 'the enemies'. See the note on this verse.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.en: he remembered the enemies in a storm
readings.plain: he remembered the enemies with a downpour

readings.w: Cairo Genizah manuscript B, folio XVIII verso, line 14 (the next word, read as 'prophet', is damaged and partly restored by Abegg)
readings.en: and he also mentioned Job
readings.plain: he also made mention of Job

why: The Plain follows the Greek, the base text. The Hebrew gives good sense: Ezekiel names Job in Ezekiel 14:14 and 14:20, and the Greek translator may have read איוב 'Job' as אויב 'enemy'.
b: In manuscript B the middle of the second line is lost; Abegg and Parker restore it as 'who maintained all the ways of righteousness', where the Greek has 'and did good to those who walk straight paths'.

a: He comforted Jacob
p: Vaticanus makes the verb singular; Alexandrinus, manuscript B and the Latin make the twelve prophets the ones who comforted and rescued.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.en: and he comforted Jacob
readings.plain: He comforted Jacob

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (Swete's notes: παρεκαλεσαν, ελυτρωσαντο; γαρ for δε, also in a corrector of Sinaiticus); Latin Vulgate (49:12) 'nam corroboraverunt Jacob, et redemerunt se'; manuscript B 'who restored Jacob' (אשר החלימו את יעקב) 'and saved him' (וישעוהו), folio XVIII verso, line 16
readings.en: for they comforted Jacob
readings.plain: For they comforted Jacob

why: The Plain keeps Vaticanus, where 'he' is most naturally God. Alexandrinus and the Hebrew make the Twelve the ones who comforted Israel, which fits the line before.

a: a people holy to the Lord
t: A holy people or a holy temple?
p: The Greek says they raised up 'a holy people'; manuscript B and the Latin have 'a holy temple'.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.en: raised up a people holy to the Lord
readings.plain: a people holy to the Lord

readings.w: Cairo Genizah manuscript B, folio XIX recto, line 1 (היכל קדש); Latin Vulgate 'templum sanctum'
readings.en: and they raised a holy temple
readings.plain: a temple holy to the Lord

why: The Plain follows the Greek. In Greek laon 'people' and naon 'temple' differ by one letter, and the Hebrew and Latin suggest 'temple' stood here first; Swete's notes also show Alexandrinus garbling the word (αον).

a: Long remembered too is Nehemiah,
p: Vaticanus has 'they hand on' (nemousin) where the other witnesses have Nehemiah's name (Neemiou).

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus and a corrector of Sinaiticus (Swete's notes: Νεεμιου); manuscript B 'Nehemiah, may his memory be glorious' (נחמיה יאדר זכרו); Latin 'Et Nehemias'
readings.orig: καὶ Νεεμίου ἐπὶ πολὺ τὸ μνημόσυνον
readings.en: and of Nehemiah the memory is great
readings.plain: Long remembered too is Nehemiah,

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.orig: καὶ νέμουσιν ἐπὶ πολὺ τὸ μνημόσυνον
readings.en: and they hand on at length the memory
readings.plain: Long they hand on the memory

why: The Plain departs from Vaticanus. Its nemousin is a copyist's slip for Neemiou, 'of Nehemiah', which the Hebrew, Alexandrinus and the Latin confirm.

a: Joseph was born a man,
p: Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus and manuscript B ask whether anyone was ever born like Joseph.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.en: and Joseph was born a man
readings.plain: Joseph was born a man,

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus (Swete's notes: ουδε ως); manuscript B 'Was a man ever born like Joseph?' (כיוסף אם נולד גבר)
readings.en: nor was a man born like Joseph
readings.plain: Nor was a man ever born like Joseph,

why: The Plain keeps Vaticanus, which makes sense. The other reading, backed by the Hebrew, continues the comparison of 49:14 ('no one like Enoch') and may be the older text.

a: Among humans Shem and Seth won honor
t: Shem and Seth, or Enosh too?
p: Manuscript B adds Enosh, son of Seth.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.orig: Σὴμ καὶ Σὴθ ἐν ἀνθρώποις ἐδοξάσθησαν
readings.en: Shem and Seth were honored among humans
readings.plain: Among humans Shem and Seth won honor

readings.w: Cairo Genizah manuscript B, folio XIX recto, line 6
readings.en: and Shem and Seth and Enosh were cared for
readings.plain: Shem, Seth and Enosh were cared for

why: The Plain follows the Greek, the base text. Enosh is Seth's son (Genesis 4:26).

a: Simon son of Onias, the high priest,
t: Simon son of Onias, or of Yohanan
p: Manuscript B opens with praise and gives the father's name as Yohanan.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (300s AD), as printed by Swete (the first hands of Vaticanus and Sinaiticus spell Ιονιου, corrected to Ονιου)
readings.orig: Σίμων Ὀνίου υἱὸς ἱερεὺς ὁ μέγας
readings.en: Simon, son of Onias, the great priest
readings.plain: Simon son of Onias, the high priest,

readings.w: Cairo Genizah manuscript B, folio XIX recto, line 7
readings.en: greatest of his brothers and glory of his people, Simon son of Yohanan, the priest
readings.plain: The greatest of his brothers and his people's glory, Simon son of Yohanan, the priest,

why: The Plain follows the Greek. Manuscript B's 'Yohanan' stands where the Greek has Onias, so the translator took Onias as the Greek form of the family name.

a: they cut a pool to hold water
p: Swete's Greek says the reservoir 'was made smaller', which makes little sense; manuscript B says it 'was dug'.

readings.w: Cairo Genizah manuscript B, folio XIX recto, line 9
readings.en: in whose generation a reservoir was dug
readings.plain: they cut a pool to hold water

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.en: a reservoir of waters was made less
readings.plain: a pool to hold water was made smaller

why: The Plain departs from the Greek. Swete's ēlattōthē means 'was lessened', which does not fit a builder's praise; the Hebrew נכרה, 'was dug', gives the sense the context needs, and the Greek word may be a copyist's slip.
b: In the second line Alexandrinus has lakkos, 'a cistern', for chalkos, 'bronze', a difference of two letters; Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus also read the plural 'reservoirs' (αποδοχεια, -χια) (Swete's notes). Manuscript B's second half, אשיח בם בהמונו, has no word for 'sea'; Abegg and Parker translate it 'the pool in them in its vastness'. See the note on this verse.

a: when the days are new
p: The Greek has 'in days of new (ones)'; the Latin has 'in the days of spring'; manuscript B has a different line.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (300s AD), as printed by Swete; Swete's notes give no difference here
readings.en: in days of new (ones)
readings.plain: when the days are new

readings.w: Latin Vulgate (50:8)
readings.orig: quasi flos rosarum in diebus vernis
readings.en: like the flower of roses in the days of spring
readings.plain: like rose blossoms in the spring days

readings.w: Cairo Genizah manuscript B, folio XIX recto, line 15 (Abegg and Parker: 'Like the branches of trees blossoming in their season')
readings.en: like the blossom of branches in the days of the set time
readings.plain: like branches in blossom in their season

why: The Plain follows the Greek. Its neōn, 'of new (ones)', may mean the new season of the year, which is how the Latin took it.

a: And now bless God, all of you,
p: Vaticanus calls 'all of you' to bless God; Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus and the KJV have 'the God of all'.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.orig: καὶ νῦν εὐλογήσατε τῷ θεῷ πάντες
readings.en: and now bless God, all of you
readings.plain: And now bless God, all of you,

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus (Swete's notes: παντων); KJV 'Now therefore bless ye the God of all'
readings.orig: καὶ νῦν εὐλογήσατε τῷ θεῷ πάντων
readings.en: and now bless the God of all
readings.plain: And now bless the God of all,

why: The Plain keeps Vaticanus. The KJV's 'God of all', which Rinkart's hymn took up (see the note), comes from the other codices. Manuscript B has 'Now bless the LORD, the God of Israel'.

a: May he entrust his mercy to us,
t: A prayer for us, or for Simon?
p: Manuscript B prays for Simon and the covenant of Phinehas; the Greek prays for 'us'. Covers the whole verse.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.orig: ἐνπιστεῦσαι μεθ᾽ ἡμῶν τὸ ἔλεος αὐτοῦ
readings.en: to entrust his mercy with us
readings.plain: May he entrust his mercy to us,

readings.w: Cairo Genizah manuscript B, folio XX recto, lines 3–4
readings.en: may his loyal love stay faithful to Simon
readings.plain: May his loyal love stay faithful to Simon, and may he keep for him the covenant of Phinehas, never to be cut off for him or his offspring as long as the heavens last;

why: The Plain follows the Greek, whose infinitive 'to entrust' it gives as a prayer. The Hebrew יאמן means 'may it be faithful'. The Hebrew may be the earlier form, written while Simon's family still held the office; that is an inference (see the note on this verse).
b: With the Hebrew reading, the next line of the Greek ('and may he set us free in his time') has no counterpart in manuscript B.

a: those who live on the hill of Samaria
p: The Greek has 'the hill of Samaria'; manuscript B and the Latin have Seir, the land of Edom.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.en: those dwelling on the mountain of Samaria
readings.plain: those who live on the hill of Samaria

readings.w: Cairo Genizah manuscript B, folio XX recto, line 6
readings.en: the inhabitants of Seir
readings.plain: those who live in Seir

readings.w: Latin Vulgate (50:28 in its numbering)
readings.en: those who live on Mount Seir
readings.plain: those who live on Mount Seir

why: The Plain follows the Greek. The Hebrew and the Latin name Seir, the Edomites south of Judea, so the three nations lie south (Edom), west (the Philistines) and north (Shechem). The Greek makes the first and third both Samaritan.

a: I, Jesus son of Sirach Eleazar, of Jerusalem,
p: The Greek names Jesus son of Sirach Eleazar of Jerusalem; one hand of Sinaiticus calls him a priest; manuscript B names Simeon son of Jeshua son of Eleazar son of Sira.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.orig: Ἰησοῦς υἱὸς Σειρὰχ Ἐλεαζὰρ ὁ Ἰεροσολυμείτης
readings.en: Jesus son of Sirach Eleazar the Jerusalemite
readings.plain: I, Jesus son of Sirach Eleazar, of Jerusalem,

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus, first hand (Swete's notes: ιερευς ο Σολυμειτης)
readings.orig: Ἰησοῦς υἱὸς Σειρὰκ Ἐλεαζὰρ ἱερεὺς ὁ Σολυμείτης
readings.en: Jesus son of Sirak Eleazar, the priest, the Solymite
readings.plain: I, Jesus son of Sirach Eleazar, the priest of Jerusalem,

readings.w: Cairo Genizah manuscript B, folio XX recto, line 7
readings.orig: לשמעון בן ישוע בן אלעזר בן סירא
readings.en: of Simeon son of Yeshua son of Eleazar son of Sira
readings.plain: I, Simeon son of Jeshua son of Eleazar son of Sira,

why: The Plain follows the Greek. The order 'son of Sirach Eleazar' is odd, and many take it to mean Jesus, son of Eleazar, of the family of Sira. The Greek name Jesus is Hebrew Yeshua (Jeshua). Manuscript B adds Simeon before him, perhaps by confusion with Simon in 50:1; its own subscription (after 51:30) says 'Simeon son of Jeshua, who is called Ben Sira'.
b: The first hand of Sinaiticus calls him 'the priest'; a corrector restored 'Jerusalemite'. Nothing else in the book says he was a priest.

a: the light of the Lord is his path
t: Light, or the fear of the Lord?
p: The Greek says 'the light of the Lord is his footstep'; manuscript B, 'the fear of the LORD is life'.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.en: the light of the Lord is his track
readings.plain: the light of the Lord is his path

readings.w: Cairo Genizah manuscript B, folio XX recto, line 10
readings.en: for the fear of the LORD is life
readings.plain: the fear of the LORD is life

why: The Plain follows the Greek. The Hebrew ends the book's main body with its theme, the fear of the LORD (1:11–20), as Proverbs 14:27 says the fear of the LORD is a fountain of life.

a: My soul came close to dying;
t: Came near to death, or praised until death?
p: Vaticanus reads 'my soul praised until death'; Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus and manuscript B, 'my soul drew near to death'.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus (Swete's notes: ηγγισεν); manuscript B 'my soul reached death' (ותגע למות נפשי), folio XX verso, line 1
readings.orig: ἤγγισεν ἕως θανάτου ἡ ψυχή μου
readings.en: my soul drew near to death
readings.plain: My soul came close to dying;

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.orig: ᾔνεσεν ἕως θανάτου ἡ ψυχή μου
readings.en: my soul praised until death
readings.plain: My soul gave praise until death;

why: The Plain departs from Vaticanus. Its ēnesen 'praised' differs by a few letters from ēngisen 'drew near', and only 'drew near' fits the next line, 'my life was right beside Hades'.

a: the Lord, the Father of my lord,
t: The Father of my lord, or 'You are my Father'?
p: The Greek calls on 'the Lord, the Father of my lord'; manuscript B has 'I exalted the LORD: You are my Father'.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (300s AD), as printed by Swete; KJV 'the Father of my Lord'
readings.en: the Lord, father of my lord
readings.plain: the Lord, the Father of my lord,

readings.w: Cairo Genizah manuscript B, folio XX verso, line 6
readings.en: and I exalted the LORD: 'You are my Father'
readings.plain: the LORD: 'You are my Father,'

why: The Plain follows the Greek. The Hebrew uses the words of Psalm 89:26, and its sense is simpler. See the note on 'the Father of my lord' for the Christian reading of the Greek.

a: I kept close watch on how I acted
t: 'In my doing' or 'in the doing of hunger'?
p: Vaticanus has an obscure 'in the doing of hunger'; Alexandrinus has 'in my doing'.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (Swete's notes: μου for λιμου)
readings.en: and in my doing I was exact
readings.plain: I kept close watch on how I acted

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.en: in the doing of hunger I was exact
readings.plain: I was exact in the doing of hunger

why: The Plain departs from Vaticanus, whose limou, 'of hunger', is hard to make sense of; it may be a slip, unless it means fasting. Alexandrinus's mou gives a plain sense.
b: The Hebrew is quite different and has nothing like 'the doing of hunger'. 11QPs-a, column XXI, lines 15–16, has חריתי נפשי בה, 'I burned with desire for her', and ופני לוא השיבותי, 'and I did not turn my face away' (some letters damaged); manuscript B, folio XXI recto, line 15, has חשקה נפשי בה ופני לא אהפך ממנה, 'my soul longed for her, and I will not turn my face from her'. The Greek 'up high' (πρὸς ὕψος) may answer to 11QPs-a's 'her heights' (וברומיה) in the next line.

a: I won a heart with her
p: Vaticanus has 'with them'; Alexandrinus 'with her' (wisdom). Manuscript B: 'I gained a heart for her'.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (Swete's notes: μετ αυτης; Sinaiticus abbreviates the word); manuscript B 'I gained a heart for her from her beginning' (ולב קניתי לה מתחלתה)
readings.en: I gained a heart with her
readings.plain: I won a heart with her

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.en: I gained a heart with them
readings.plain: I won a heart with them

why: The Plain departs from Vaticanus. The whole poem speaks of wisdom as 'her', and 'them' has nothing to refer to.
b: 11QPs-a, column XXI, line 16, begins this verse טרתי נפשי בה וברומיה לוא: a verb of uncertain sense, then 'my soul on her, and in her heights... not', and the rest of the line is damaged. Manuscript B, folio XXI recto, line 18, has ובטהרה מצאתיה, 'and in purity I found her', which agrees with the Greek 'by cleansing I found her'.
